transcript.text: Every time I put the oven on it runs for a few minutes and then the trip switch goes and half the house loses power. Reset it 3 times tonight. Hotpoint built-in, about 9 years old. What could cause this?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. The most likely cause is a heating element that's leaking to earth. As an element ages its internal insulation can break down, and the leakage gets worse as it heats up. That fits an oven that runs fine for a few minutes and then trips. At 9 years old that's a very common failure. In rough order of likelihood:
1. A heating element leaking to earth. The base element is a frequent culprit, especially if anything has spilled onto it, but the fan or grill element can do it too. Because the elements share wiring, the function you're using doesn't prove which element is at fault.
2. A burnt or damp terminal connector, or chafed wiring touching the metal casing, inside the oven.
3. Less likely, a scorched mains terminal block where the supply cable connects at the back. It isn't the thermostat. A thermostat fault makes the oven go cold; it doesn't trip the house electrics. What you have is an earth fault. Please don't reset it and try again. Each trip is the safety device stopping a fault current, and the oven shouldn't be used until an engineer or electrician has checked it. Switch it off at the cooker isolator (the big switch on the wall near the oven), or at the consumer unit if you'd rather. Finding the leaking element needs proper insulation testing, so it's a job for a qualified engineer rather than an owner check. Two things you can note without powering it, which will help the engineer:
1. Does it trip on more than one function (fan oven, grill, conventional), or only one?
2. Has there been any spillage onto the oven floor, or a recent deep clean? Moisture or burnt-on spills can make an element leak, and that points towards the base element. If you notice a burning smell or any scorch marks near the back where the cable connects, mention that too, as it points to the terminal block. The good news is that a replacement element is usually a reasonably priced repair, so on a 9-year-old built-in oven it's normally worth fixing rather than replacing.

Thank you, I won't reset it again. To answer your questions: it trips every time on the fan oven setting, but I ran the grill on its own once for 10 minutes and it didn't trip. I also cleaned the oven with oven spray the weekend before this started. There's been no burning smell, bang or sparks.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
That's really useful, and it narrows things down a lot. The fan oven setting normally powers the circular element behind the back panel and the fan motor. The grill ran for 10 minutes without tripping, which makes the grill element much less likely. So the leading suspect is the fan oven element leaking to earth. I'd put it at fairly likely, not certain. The timing of the cleaning matters too. Oven spray, or the water used to rinse it off, can creep through the fan cover or round the back panel onto the element ends and their connectors. The connectors then start leaking current to the metal casing as they heat up. Sometimes that only finishes off an element that was already weak after 9 years. 1. The fan oven element leaking to earth. This is the most likely.
2. Cleaner residue or damp on the element terminals or wiring behind the back panel.
3. Less likely, the fan motor itself, or the base element tripping on a shared circuit. Because elements share wiring, the function that trips isn't absolute proof. An engineer can tell these apart with an insulation test on each element and on the fan motor, with everything disconnected. That isn't an owner job. There were no smells, sparks or scorching, which is reassuring and makes the mains terminal block unlikely. 1. Look through the fan cover and around the edges of the back panel for any cleaner residue or white crusting. If you see some, tell the engineer, as it supports the cleaner theory. Don't try to clean inside or remove any panels.
2. Find the model number for the engineer. It's on the rating plate, usually on the edge of the frame when you open the door. If it's confirmed, a fan oven element is usually a straightforward, reasonably priced repair, so it's well worth doing on this oven.

I can't see the fan element without taking the back panel off, and I'm not willing to do that. As for the model number, the rating label is hidden by the trim when the door is shut. If I push it, I can faintly make out 'SI6' and something after it, but I can't read the rest. Is that enough for the engineer, or is there another way to find the full number?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
'SI6' on its own isn't quite enough. Hotpoint uses that kind of prefix across several ovens, and the engineer will want the full model number, and ideally the serial number, to be sure of getting the right element first time. It's not a problem, though. An engineer can read the plate on the visit, so you don't have to find it. If you'd like to have it ready, here are a few easy ways to try: 1. Take a photo instead of reading it. With the oven off at the isolator and cold, open the door fully, shine your phone torch at the plate and photograph it from an angle, then zoom in on the photo. A camera often picks up print the eye can't, and it saves you holding the trim back.
2. Check the paperwork. The full model number is usually printed on the front of the instruction manual, the guarantee card, the original receipt, or the kitchen fitter's or installer's invoice.
3. If you registered the oven with Hotpoint when it was new, the model may be on your account, or on a confirmation email from back then. Please don't pull the oven out of its housing to get at a label on the side or back. Being built in, it's wired in and heavy, and the engineer can do that safely if it's needed. Not taking the back panel off is completely fine. That's the engineer's job anyway. They'll insulation-test the fan element, the fan motor and the other elements separately. That will show whether it's the fan oven element itself (still my main suspect), damp or cleaner residue on its connections, or something on a shared circuit. Until then, keep the oven off at the isolator. When you book, it's worth telling them it trips the house electrics on fan oven after a few minutes but the grill ran for 10 minutes without tripping, and that it was cleaned with oven spray just before the fault started. That gives them a head start.

candidates: A heating element leaking to earth (base, fan or grill element; the base element is a common culprit) (high)
Element terminal connector or internal wiring shorting to the chassis (medium)
Burnt mains terminal block or supply connection (low)
